title: Designing a ‘Hunger Games’ Prequel: From Using 600,000 Flowers in the ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ Arena to Recreating the Capitol in the 1970s
description: Production designer Uli Hanisch thought shooting the highly anticipated “Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” in the remote town of Asturias, Spai
body:
Production designer Uli Hanisch thought shooting the highly anticipated “Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” in the remote town of Asturias, Spain, meant they would be safe from spoilers. The production would shoot in a desolate valley, requiring an hours-long trek to the set, plus the lack of hotel accommodations and the occasional restaurant nearby, reassured him. Until it happened.

	“We had the experience from last time where fans were following us to Poland trying to take pictures, but up there, it’s nothing, it’s just us,” Hanisch tells Variety. “We were starting to build up the cornucopia pieces, and I think after two or three days, the first images appeared on the internet. It was somebody saying, ‘Oh, we found them.’ I was like, ‘How is that even possible?’”
	

	Even though sleuthing fans were able to find it, the location is so secluded that Hanisch wondered if it would be feasible to get a crew of the necessary magnitude all the way up there. But once he saw the luscious greenery contrasting the jagged mountains, he knew they had found the arena for the Second Quarter Quell, and they’d have to make it work.

	“I stepped out of the car and looked into the valley and said, ‘God damn, yeah, that’s it,’” Hanisch says. “I sent an image to Francis [Lawrence, the franchise’s longtime director], saying, ‘Look, this is our valley, but it’s really far away.’ And he said, ‘Yeah, well, we have to do it here.’”

	The next step was designing and building the Cornucopia — the focal point of the arena, which distinguishes each iteration of the Hunger Games (and each installment of the film franchise) from the others. Similar to the paradoxical landscape, Hanisch and his team wanted to create something that balanced beauty with danger. They landed on a blossom with metal spikes for petals, surrounded by thick beds of wildflowers, arranged by color, demarking each tribute’s position around the centerpiece.
	



	

					The Cornucopia in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”
									Courtesy of Lionsgate
	



	“It’s very beautiful, it’s very elegant, but it also looks very deadly and evil,” Hanisch says. “When they were shooting the opening, and the tributes were all around with these capes, I thought this looked like one of those satanic, strange cults. I thought it was actually a very matching feel.”

	Once the games begin and the tributes abandon the menacing structure, they are fully immersed in a flourishing woodland environment where the foliage is as deadly as it is extravagant. To bring this to life, Hanisch’s small but mighty team of six worked for three weeks dressing the arena with flowers. The arrangements surrounding the Cornucopia alone required up to 600,000 artificial flowers.

	“We underestimated it. What you see in the movie is still enhanced by visual effects,” Hansich says.

	The team also had to invent deceptively beautiful devices like the berms: a mechanical bush that serves as a portal for mutts to enter and exit the arena, and a conduit for Haymitch (Joseph Zada) to destroy it.

	“Oh, the berms!” Hanisch coos. “The berms were really special because, first of all, what is a berm? We have to come up with some kind of a sensible thing on our own to make it work. It’s hard to tell that as an interesting story because it’s a very long, time-consuming, tiring process.”



	

					Concept art from “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping”
	





	

					District 12 in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.” 
									Courtesy of Lionsgate
	



	While testing the limits of his imagination and portraying the grandeur of the games posed significant production challenges for Hanisch, recreating District 12 was like “coming home.” The cast and crew returned to the same abandoned steel mill factory in Germany where they shot the 2023 prequel “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” and once again captured the dreariness of the downtrodden district.

	“We agreed that District 12 never changes, which I like very much,” Hanisch says. He may be partial, though, because filming took place near his hometown of Nuremberg. “It’s very beautiful, actually, very intense and complex. I know every corner there.”

	Recreating Panem’s Capitol didn’t have the fond feeling of going home, but it was familiar and a task that Hanisch holds “close and dear.” With the 2023 prequel “The Battle of Songbirds and Snakes,” the filmmakers decided that the Capitol would be based on Berlin after World War II because “we can see what the situation has done to the city,” Hanisch explains. The timeline for “Sunrise on the Reaping” jumped 20 years into the future, landing in a 1970s aesthetic. “We wanted to explore the capital of Panem at the peak of its power, wealth and arrogance,” he says. So, production returned to the heart of the historic city for its “glorious,” “unique” architecture and its ability to capture the power dynamics they were looking for.
	

	“[Berlin’s International Congress Center] looks like a Star Wars spaceship landed in the middle of the city,” Hanisch says. “It’s huge, it has this strange futuristic ’70s approach, it’s abandoned, and we’ve been there before. We were circling around with all our ideas, and then we were like, ‘Oh my God, we have that thing standing there,’ and you realize you can cover a third of the movie and the heart of the capital in this one go.”



	

	





	

					Scenes from the Capitol in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” filmed in Berlin.
									Murray Close/Lionsgate
	



	Along with the city’s physical assets, emulating the opulence of the ’70s was a choice rooted in the same principle as the arena: that beneath the beauty lies danger.

	“The ’70s in the Western world are supposed to be in our memory, this progressive time when things started to change with this youth rebellion, but if you look at the ’70s, it was the peak of Western wealth,” Hanisch says. “Besides this angle of the youth rebelling against all of that, the rest of society was extremely saturated. They were proud, untouchable and wealthy in style. That’s why we thought that’s an interesting twist to show. We see something, and we have an idea of what it means, but now all of a sudden it’s the opposite.”

	The ’70s imagery resulted from Hanisch and the filmmakers’ interpretation of Suzanne Collins’ novel and then Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie’s screenplay. He acknowledges that it is already a challenge to translate books into movies because they are such different art forms, but it’s more difficult, impossible even, to value people’s different interpretations of the material.

	“Every reader creates their own world while reading it, and you can never say your version is right and your friend’s version is wrong, so we cannot do anything else but what we think is right,” Hanisch says. “It’s more about dealing with the intention of the writer of the novel and then translating it into what you think is right.”

	This motto keeps Hanisch grounded when dealing with such a massive, devoted fan base: “What more can you do?”

	“We always think a lot about the fans,” Hanisch says. “I find it so fascinating how important this is for so many people and how seriously they talk and think about it. It’s not really for us. Of course, it’s my job, and I love to do that, and it’s a fantastic thing to be done, but it is mainly to make the fans happy. And they should be happy.”

title: Oscars: 38 Animated Movies, 104 International Films and 190 Documentaries Make the Eligibility Lists, Setting New Records

		Oscars: 38 Animated Movies, 104 International Films and 190 Documentaries Make the Eligibility Lists
body:
Nov 23, 2026 11:00am PT	
	

	
		Oscars: 38 Animated Movies, 104 International Films and 190 Documentaries Make the Eligibility Lists, Setting New Records
	
	
			


			
			
	

									AMPAS / Netflix / A24 / Pixar
	

		
	
				

	The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences has released the lists of films eligible for animated feature, documentary feature and international feature at the 99th Academy Awards, and two of the three are setting records. Animated feature has 38 eligible films, the most in the category’s history. International feature has 104, also a record. Documentary feature comes in at 190.

	Pixar’s “Toy Story 5” and Universal and Illumination’s “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” lead a group of studio billion-dollar tentpoles that also includes “Minions & Monsters,” “Tangles” and “Wildwood.” They come alongside Ketchup Entertainment’s “Coyote vs. Acme,” a movie plenty of people wondered if they’d ever get to see, and the return of a familiar property with GKids’ “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom.”
	

	Don’t overlook the international animated titles that have demonstrated pockets of support. Japan enters the race with “Cosmic Princess Kaguya!,” “All You Need Is Kill” and “Mobile Suit Gundam Hathaway: The Sorcery of Nymph Circe,” while Mexico offers the stop-motion feature “I Am Frankelda” and Spain brings “Decorado.”

	The Academy notes that some still need to complete their required theatrical runs and meet the category’s other rules before they can advance. Animation branch members vote automatically for the five nominees. Members of other branches can opt in, as long as they meet a minimum viewing requirement. Animated features can also compete in other categories, best picture included, and a country’s official international feature submission can be considered for animated feature.
	

	On the documentary side, the 190 films cover just about everything: music, politics, art, sports and true crime. The contenders include “Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie,” “Ask E. Jean,” “Marc by Sofia,” “Avedon,” “Lorne,” “Musk,” “The AI Doc: Or How I Became an Apocaloptimist,” “EPiC: Elvis Presley in Concert,” “Billy Preston: That’s the Way God Planned It,” “Man on the Run,” “Free Leonard Peltier,” “The Trial of Alec Baldwin” and “My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile.”

	One of the biggest titles that pundits will be keeping their eyes on is Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s “You Can See Everything,” the A24 cultural sensation that just surpassed $100 million globally, a rare box office milestone for a documentary.

	Some docs also still need to finish their qualifying runs. Films that won a qualifying festival award or were submitted as a country’s official international feature selection are eligible as well, and that crossover is all over this year’s lists. Fourteen titles show up in both races, among them Palestine’s “Citizen Osama,” the United Kingdom’s “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” Ukraine’s “Traces,” Iceland’s “The Ground beneath Our Feet,” Switzerland’s “Who Is Still Alive” and Albania’s “State Film.”

	The Documentary branch picks both the shortlist of 15 and the eventual five nominees.

	In international feature, 100 of the 104 films were submitted by countries or regions. The other four got in through the Academy’s festival award pathway: Berlin Golden Bear winner “Yellow Letters,” Sundance World Cinema Grand Jury Prize (Dramatic) winner “Shame and Money,” Busan Award for best film winner “Midday Meal” and Toronto Platform Award winner “Angh.” The Cannes Palme d’Or winner “Fjord” was also the official selection of Romania.

	Official submissions include France’s “Minotaur,” Spain’s “La Bola Negra,” Brazil’s “Gugu’s World,” Norway’s “Growth of the Soil,” Germany’s “Everytime,” Italy’s “The Spiral,” Japan’s “All of a Sudden,” South Korea’s “Possible Love,” Mexico’s “On the Road,” Denmark’s “Woman Unknown,” Iran’s “Land of Angels,” India’s “Gondhal” and Canada’s “Nina Roza.”
	

	To qualify, an international feature must run longer than 40 minutes, be produced outside the United States and have dialogue that’s more than 50% non-English. Members from every branch can opt in to the preliminary round if they meet the minimum viewing requirement. That shortlist also lands Dec. 15.Preliminary voting for select categories runs Monday, Dec. 7, through Friday, Dec. 11. Shortlists follow Tuesday, Dec. 15, and nominations will be announced Thursday, Jan. 21, 2027.

	The 99th Oscars take place Sunday, March 14, 2027, at the Dolby Theatre at Ovation Hollywood. The ceremony airs live on ABC, streams live on Hulu and reaches more than 200 territories worldwide.

	The full lists of eligible films are below.

body:
From “Stranger Things” to virtually any Trader Joe’s, new wave music is inescapable. Not only are bands like B-52s, Duran Duran, Tears for Fears and Billy Idol still frequently touring, new generations are embracing the danceable sounds of 1977 to 1987, whether the tunes are making shoppers dance at your local Trader Joe’s or soundtracking a nostalgia-tinged TV series.

	How has the genre managed to hang on for so long, even as rock is no longer the dominant sound across the music scene? The new docuseries “New Wave,” premiering Monday on MGM+, tells the story of how a loosely connected group of misfits, fashionistas and punk rockers from the U.K. and U.S. coalesced to form a movement — and how the dawn of music videos then propelled that music into the stratosphere.
	

	In the doc, musicians, DJs and veejays (Martha Quinn! Mark Goodman!) consider the ingredients that created the movement: the influence of women, the colorful and original fashions of the era and the dawn of MTV, all coming together to create a joyful decade of energetic music that still resonates today.

	Interviews in the four-part series include Kate Pierson and Fred Schneider of the B52s, Billy Idol, Mark Mothersbaugh of Devo, Danny Elfman of Oingo Boingo, Stewart Copeland of the Police, John Taylor of Duran Duran, Curt Smith of Tears for Fears, Johnny Marr of the Smiths, Kathy Valentine of the Go-Gos, Brian Setzer of Stray Cats and Jim Kerr of Simple Minds.

	New wave torchbearer Richard Blade, the KROQ and Sirius First Wave DJ who has helped keep fans engaged with the sound ever since it started, serves as consulting producer, with Douglas Tirola directing. R.J. Cutler and Elise Pearlstein are among the executive producers. The production company is This Machine Filmworks, a part of Sony Pictures Television.
	

	Speaking with Variety, the B52s’ Pierson and the creative team broke down how new wave got started and labeled, how the series was put together and why the music has endured so long.
	
		Why did you think new wave needed its own documentary series? 	

	Douglas Tirola: The idea was that by telling this story, we would sort of defend new wave. I think a lot of people think of it as a keyboard, two people, a synthesizer, and a band from Britain making quirky dance music. It’s so much more than that. New wave brought the alternative into the mainstream. It changed music, movies, TV, design, fashion, politics, and how we look at and go out with one another.

	Everybody loves the music of their youth; it’s their soundtrack, and it’s nostalgic to them. I felt there was a belief system behind new wave, and that’s what the story set out to show.

	Elise Pearlstein: New wave was a short period — really only about 10 years — but so much music was created and the culture changed during that time. There had never really been a documentary that looked specifically at new wave, so we all thought it was high time.
	
		The term new wave in regards to music is often credited to Sire Records founder Seymour Stein. Why did it need its own term, and what did the bands have in common?	

	Pearlstein: It was really a marketing term. New wave artists were originally grouped with punk, and punk wasn’t commercial. Some venues didn’t want punk acts to play because they would destroy the place. So “new wave” was a marketing term created to distinguish new wave artists from the punk movement and, ultimately, make them more commercially viable. And it worked.

	Kate Pierson: I really think it’s a made-up term trying to encompass post-punk. Punk was just evolving; this was a sort of evolution from punk. The whole idea was that you could express yourself in any way, and anyone could do it. I think the thing about new wave that changed from punk was that it was inclusive. There were a lot more women, queer artists and Black artists in the scene.

	Having a mixed band, with queer men and women in it, made us very different and unique in that scene. But it really fit into the whole new-wave fashion: it was fashion-forward and had eclectic influences. There was also technology — the addition of synthesizers and electronic music.
	

	Every band was so different from the others. New wave embraced all these different styles: danceable music, funky music, even some disco influences. We loved disco.
	
		Doug, your previous project was about Leonard Bernstein, from a much earlier time. Why did this era lend itself much more to making a very visual documentary?	

	Tirola: There were more people running around with video cameras, even if they were big. With the explosion of cable, more people were producing content, even if it was cable access. That was a relief. Once you hit the ’80s, there’s a lot more out there.

	R.J. Cutler: It coincides with the arrival of MTV, which was a great gift to the filmmakers.

	Pearlstein: A lot of the bands came from art school. Talking Heads and the B-52s were interested in visual media and the visual medium, so they embraced visual storytelling around music. Even before making music videos, bands like Devo were playing around with film and visuals in their music.
	
		How did new wave influence style at the time?	

	Pierson: The ripped garbage-bag look that Belinda Carlisle wore, or Debbie Harry’s style — it was this fusion of punk, avant-garde style and thrift-store chic. It was very “anything goes” and experimental fashion, which was so great.

	I think we (the B-52s) made an impact visually, so MTV embraced us, and that helped a lot.
	
		How did you come up with the throughline of the series, which tells the story of the rise and fall and rise of new wave?	

	Pearlstein: Because it’s a pretty tight chronology — it’s only a 10-year period — we looked at the arc of new wave. It went from obscurity to a pretty fast demise within that time. We looked at how it broke out and became mainstream, how it peaked and jumped the shark, and then how it dissipated.

	We also looked at milestones, like the synthesizer, which democratized the ability to make this kind of music, and MTV. Bob Geldof’s Band Aid and Live Aid were important moments when everybody came together, and you saw the diversity of the music as well as its commitment to change.

	Then new wave started showing up in ads and getting co-opted by the mainstream. Ultimately, it was parodied. Once it got too extreme, some artists, like U2, didn’t want to be associated with new wave; they wanted to be beyond a genre. 
	

	Cutler: The fundamental story of outsiders becoming insiders is a great landscape for dramatic storytelling.

	Tirola: Richard Blade was an absolute resource throughout this entire thing. He helped us get some of the interviews, gave us information, and gave us some of the key plot points. One point was when new wave took off. Richard talked about three songs that came out in a short period of time. One was Gary Numan’s “Cars.” I’d never put those three songs together that way before.

	New wave took the place of disco. Then, when some things didn’t work out, the industry said, “No, we don’t want New Wave,” and then it had a comeback.
	
		What were some of your favorite interviews in the series?	

	Tirola: I thought John Taylor was incredible. He said during the interview, “Thank God someone’s finally making this.” (Kate Pierson) also understood what new wave was: it was for outsiders, but outsiders who wanted to be in the mainstream. Every interview was great, but that one was special. Billy Idol, who I was a fan of but had never met, was so insightful and detail-oriented. He understood the bigger idea we were going for: where new wave fits into the big picture.



	

					Bono of U2 performs at the US Festival, a major California event which helped bring new wave music into the mainstream.
									Redferns
	


	
		Who would you have liked to get but weren’t able to? 	

	Tirola: U2 comes to mind. I feel like Bono and their early story would have been interesting. I think people forget they weren’t always a stadium band.

	Richard Blade: When U2 played at the US Festival, they were a small band. If you look at the running order, they opened for Missing Persons. Bono went to climb the speaker stacks and wave his rebel flag, as he liked to do at concerts, and security grabbed his leg and pulled him down: “What do you think you’re doing? Get down from there!” Back then, he was just this scruffy little Irish guy trying to climb the speaker stacks. It’s amazing to see them go from that to perhaps the biggest rock band in the world
	
		You still hear new wave music everywhere, especially in movies and TV shows. How has it managed to endure so long? Are younger people embracing new wave?	

	Blade: The younger generation is growing up with it now because it’s been used so many times in commercials. If you watch an NFL game, every third commercial — if it’s not Peyton Manning selling something — has an ’80s song playing. “Stranger Things” was the perfect example of that, and so many shows followed its influence on the ’80s.
	

	It’s not just the parents, and it’s not going to fade away as we get older. People will continue to love Depeche Mode, The Cure and Duran Duran, just as people love the Beatles, The Who, The Beach Boys and The Rolling Stones.

	Pearlstein: The B-52s really epitomize that (staying power). The music is fun, danceable, hopeful, sticky, addictive — and it makes you feel good.

	I also think 20-somethings today have rediscovered New Wave in a huge way. The gender fluidity new wave embraced is back today, and the sounds, looks, and goth style are all popular again.

	Cutler: It captures the spirit of youth forever. For those of us whose youth it’s tied to, it’s always resonant, but there’s also a timelessness to its spirit of rebellion and inclusion. The combination makes it forever young, and that’s really exciting. 

	It’s still driving culture.

	(This interview has been edited and condensed.)

schema.headline: Why New Wave Music Won’t Go Away: New Documentary Explores How Synthesizers, MTV and Androgyny Built the Enduring Genre

title: Super Bowl 2027 and Jay-Z Halftime Show to Screen in Imax Theaters
description:
Can’t get a ticket to the big game? Worry not, because Imax is bringing Super Bowl LXI to the big screen.

	Imax is working with ESPN, the Walt Dis
body:
Can’t get a ticket to the big game? Worry not, because Imax is bringing Super Bowl LXI to the big screen.

	Imax is working with ESPN, the Walt Disney Company and the NFL to screen the Super Bowl in the company’s premium theaters for the first time. The game will play in hundreds of Imax venues in the United States and select international territories, marking the company’s largest-ever live event. Imax’s recent alternative programming options have included a front-row seat to the FIA Formula One World Championship.
	

	Super Bowl LXI will be held on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Calif. Imax theater tickets are expected to go on sale in January. The four-hour presentation will feature ESPN’s main game telecast and the halftime show headlined by Jay-Z, as well as pregame and postgame coverage. A promotional spot and other marketing materials for the event will appear in theaters during Thanksgiving week. Additional details, including a list of participating locations and ticketing information, will be announced in the coming weeks.

	“Watching the Super Bowl with your fellow fans is one of the great shared experiences in sports, and this first-of-its-kind collaboration with the NFL and Imax takes it to a historic new scale,” said Ken Potrock, the Walt Disney Company’s president of major event integration. “With ESPN’s first Super Bowl, we’re reaching fans across an unprecedented range of platforms and meeting them wherever they want to be, with unique moments that only Disney and ESPN can deliver.”

	Rich Gelfond, CEO of Imax, called the Super Bowl programming “a milestone for Imax that further elevates our standing as a premier global platform for entertainment and events.”
	

	“The Super Bowl is a one-of-a-kind global cultural event imbued with spectacle, sound, drama, and heroes — all the makings of a great Imax experience,” he said. “We’re excited to work in partnership with Disney, ESPN and the NFL to give football fans an unforgettable night.”

schema.headline: Super Bowl 2027 and Jay-Z Halftime Show to Screen in Imax Theaters

title: Shawn Levy’s 21 Laps Inks Rich Overall Film Deal at Sony
description:
Shawn Levy‘s 21 Laps Entertainment has signed a major overall film deal with Sony Pictures.

	21 Laps lands at Sony after a competitive process wit
body:
Shawn Levy‘s 21 Laps Entertainment has signed a major overall film deal with Sony Pictures.

	21 Laps lands at Sony after a competitive process with multiple studios bidding to get into business with the blockbuster filmmaker and his prolific production company. The rich new deal, focused on developing and producing feature films, extends across all of Sony Pictures’ labels and begins in fall 2027.


	The pact also reunites Levy with Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group chairman and CEO Tom Rothman and Motion Picture Group president Sanford Panitch. The trio’s relationship goes back more than two decades, boasting some of Levy’s early successes as a director and producer, including the “Night at the Museum” movies, “Cheaper by the Dozen” and “Date Night.”
	

	“I go ALL the way back with Shawn. We made a pile of hits together before he went on to far greater successes, none of which surprised me in the slightest,” Rothman said in a statement announcing the news.

	“His talent as a producer, director and head of the coolest creative company around, is rivaled only by his unmatched enthusiasm,” Rothman continued. “I feel lucky as hell to reunite, and excited for everyone at Sony to discover what I have long known — Shawn Levy is the real deal.”

	Levy, whose 21 Laps will celebrate its 21st anniversary next year, was equally enthused.

	“Tom, Sanford and I have a long history together, and some of the most formative and rewarding experiences of my career came during the years we worked together at Fox,” Levy said in a statement. “Tom saw the future of my career before I did, and he bet on me early and with a big-hearted (and loud!) conviction that is one of his trademarks, and for which I’ll be forever grateful.”
	

	About the future of the company, Levy added: “21 Laps was built on empowering fellow filmmakers and helping them tell stories imbued with their unique voices and visions. Along with my entire 21 Laps team, I’m thrilled to begin this next chapter with the team at Sony, and am excited about the wide-open breadth of opportunity across Sony’s many labels. I deeply value their commitment to theatrical filmmaking.”

	News of the Sony Pictures deal comes after Levy and 21 Laps set an overall TV deal at Disney‘s 20th Television in September, following a long tenure at Netflix. The watermark for the company’s TV business is, of course, executive producing Netflix’s groundbreaking and Emmy-winning series “Stranger Things.” 21 Laps will executive produce the upcoming live-action prequel series “Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure.”

	21 Laps films have grossed more than $5 billion at the worldwide box office. Recent successes include Marvel’s “Deadpool & Wolverine,” directed, produced and co-written by Levy, which grossed more than $1.3 billion worldwide, and A24’s “Backrooms,” which became the studio’s highest-grossing release worldwide. Next year, Levy will debut the much-anticipated “Star Wars: Starfighter.” The film, directed and produced by Levy and starring Ryan Gosling, will launch in theaters on May 28, 2027. Levy will then reteam with Gosling and Marvel for “Ghost Rider,” which is slated for a July 28, 2028 theatrical release.

	The company’s slate of upcoming projects also includes Universal Pictures’ romantic comedy “The Catch,” starring Emma Stone and Chris Pine; Netflix’s drama series “The Sticks,” starring Michelle Monaghan; Amazon MGM Studios’ supernatural horror film “Seasons”; Netflix’s feature comedy “One Attempt Remaining,” starring Jennifer Garner and John Cena; and an untitled Netflix spy feature starring Kevin Hart and Henry Cavill.

	Levy and 21 Laps Entertainment are represented by WME and Wendy Kirk at JSSK.

schema.headline: Shawn Levy’s 21 Laps Inks Rich Overall Film Deal at Sony

title: Taylor Swift, a Brenda Lee Superfan, Presents the Star With 10x Platinum Plaque for ‘Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree’
description: Taylor Swift has gone on record from early in her teens forward as a Brenda Lee fan, and on her recent trip to Nashville she got to honor her pred
body:
Taylor Swift has gone on record from early in her teens forward as a Brenda Lee fan, and on her recent trip to Nashville she got to honor her predecessor in country-pop crossover stardom with a plaque honoring the diamond-selling status of Lee’s “Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree.”

	Only two Christmas singles have been certified by the RIAA for selling 10 million copies, with Lee’s 1958 signature smash becoming the second, following Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You.”

	A video posted on Instagram and X shows Swift knocking on the door to a room where the 81-year-old Lee is awaiting a visitor. “No way,” Lee says, upon first being greeted. “You grow a foot?” Swift responds, “One per year, yeah.”

Got the biggest surprise ever to kick off this Rockin' season! @TaylorSwift surprised me in Nashville with a @RIAA Diamond plaque commemorating 10 million copies of "Rockin' Around The Christmas Tree". Only the second Christmas song in history to reach this milestone! 🎄 pic.twitter.com/Nl1K65EbSe— Brenda Lee (@BrendaLeeMusic_) November 23, 2026


	Getting to the matter at hand, Swift says, “ I’m one of the many, many fans of your iconic song ‘Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree.’ It is such an incredible song. And I’m not the only person who feels that way, because I’m very honored to get to present you with your diamond certification for more than 10 million copies. You recorded this when you were only 13 years old, and it is one of only two Christmas songs to ever reach this milestone. You’re in very good company with Mariah Carey, all the way at the top, and this is yours now, and it will be yours forever… On behalf of all the fans and all the families and people whose Christmases this song has absolutely added dazzle and sparkle and warmth to, thank you so much for your incredible work.”


	Lee immediately thinks of collaborators who are not around to join the celebration. “Well, the writer, Johnny Marks, who’s no longer here, would be so proud. And all the musicians and (producer) Owen Bradley, everybody, all the fans…”

	“I’m so happy to get to have this moment with you,” Swift says, noting she has “been such a fan for so long.”  “And I’m a fan,” responds Lee. “Oh, really?” “Yes. I wish you wasn’t so tall,” says Lee, who at the so-called height of her fame, when she was known as “Little Miss Dynamite,” stood at 4 feet 9 inches.


	When she was 18, Swift wrote an essay about Lee, titled “Rare Peer.” It was republished in a 2017 book in which female country artists saluted their heroes, the Holly Gleason-edited “Woman Walk the Line.”
	

	Read Variety‘s previous interview with Brenda Lee about “Rockin'” here, conducted in 2023, when the song finally reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 for the first time, after 65 years.

schema.headline: Taylor Swift, a Brenda Lee Superfan, Presents the Star With 10x Platinum Plaque for ‘Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree’

title: Steven Spielberg to Direct Western Movie Starring Cillian Murphy, Jessie Buckley; Paul Thomas Anderson to Write Script Based on ‘The Heart in Winter’
description: Steven Spielberg is set to adapt Kevin Barry’s Western novel “The Heart in Winter” for Focus Features, Variety has confirmed. Jessie Buckley, Cilli
body:
Steven Spielberg is set to adapt Kevin Barry’s Western novel “The Heart in Winter” for Focus Features, Variety has confirmed. Jessie Buckley, Cillian Murphy and Mark Rylance are set to star. Spielberg will direct with a script from “One Battle After Another” Oscar winner Paul Thomas Anderson.

	Barry’s 2024 novel follows Irish poet Tom Rourke, who falls in love with Polly Gillespie, the new bride of his town’s mine captain. Together, they take off for San Francisco with a pack of armed gunmen hot on their trail. Kristie Macosko Krieger, Sarah Murphy, Anderson and Spielberg serve as producers. Executive producers include Tim Headington, Neil Shah, Ryan Zacarias and Ana Leocha. The film is eyeing a release in 2028.
	

	“The Heart in Winter” reunites Spielberg with Universal after he released “Disclosure Day” with the studio in June. The sci-fi chase thriller opened to $44 million and went on to earn $447 million worldwide. The Western romance also reunites Spielberg and Buckley. The three-time Oscar winner produced 2025’s “Hamnet” at Focus, which earned Buckley an Academy Award for best actress.

	Anderson is hot off his success with “One Battle After Another,” which took home six statuettes at the 2025 Oscars, including Anderson’s first best director win. “The Heart in Winter” is the first film Anderson will write without serving as director. 

	Buckley most recently starred alongside Christian Bale in Maggie Gyllenhaal’s “The Bride!” for Warner Bros. Coming up for Buckley is “Hold on to Your Angels” with Paul Mescal and “Three Incestuous Sisters” with Josh O’Connor, Dakota Johnson and Saoirse Ronan. “Oppenheimer” Oscar winner Murphy recently reprised his role as British street lord Thomas Shelby in Netflix’s “Peaky Blinders” movie “The Immortal Man.” On the horizon for Murphy is “A Quiet Place Part III” and the third and final chapter of the “28 Years Later” saga. Rylance, who starred in Spielberg’s 2015 drama “Bridge of Spies,” will soon appear in Luca Guadagnino’s Sam Altman biopic “Artificial.” His directorial debut, “Nice Fish,” starring Michelle Williams, is currently in pre-production. 
	

	Buckley is repped by CAA, United Agents and Johnson Shapiro Slewett & Kole. Murphy is repped by WME and Sloane Offer Weber & Dern. Rylance is represented by CAA and Peikoff Mahan Law Office. Anderson is repped by CAA and Jackoway Austen Tyerman Wertheimer Mandelbaum Morris Bernstein Trattner Auerbach Hynick Jaime LeVine Sample & Klein.

schema.headline: Steven Spielberg to Direct Western Movie Starring Cillian Murphy, Jessie Buckley; Paul Thomas Anderson to Write Script Based on ‘The Heart in Winter’

title: American Film Institute Establishes First Full-Ride Scholarship for Production Design
description:
The American Film Institute established its first full-ride scholarship dedicated to production design.

	The AFI World Builder Scholarship for Pro
body:
The American Film Institute established its first full-ride scholarship dedicated to production design.

	The AFI World Builder Scholarship for Production Design will be awarded to an admitted fall 2027 Production Design Fellow and cover tuition across the four-semester, full-time program.

	“The AFI Conservatory has championed visual storytellers and worldbuilders for nearly 60 years, empowering thousands of filmmakers to express their unique vision,” said Susan Ruskin, Dean of the AFI Conservatory. “We’re thrilled to expand our scholarship opportunities with the first-ever AFI World Builder Scholarship for Production Design, highlighting the invaluable artistic contribution of production designers who create stunning visuals and transport audiences to new worlds.”
	

	The AFI Conservatory hosted a conversation with production design alumni as part of the announcement. Tom Hammock (AFI Class of 2004, “Weapons,” “Resident Evil”) and Claudia Ethridge (AFI Class of 2018, “Euphoria,” “The SpongeBob Movie: Search for SquarePants”) discussed why they pursued production design as a career, their experience at the Conservatory and their advice for aspiring filmmakers.

	“It really is this amazing place where independent filmmaking and studio filmmaking come together and prepare you to take either path and go off into the world and really try and create worlds for films to take place in,” Hammock said.

	Said Ethridge, “I felt very confident stepping into the film industry knowing that I went to AFI and I had created this background there that I could pull from in whatever job that I was working on.”
	

	The AFI Conservatory offers a two-year MFA in production design to prepare fellows for professional careers. Fellows collaborate on projects, design a thesis production and build a professional portfolio while in the program.

	The priority deadline to apply for the AFI World Builder Scholarship for Production Design is Dec. 1. Further information can be found on the AFI website.

schema.headline: American Film Institute Establishes First Full-Ride Scholarship for Production Design

title: ‘Way of the Warrior Kid’ Review: Chris Pratt Pulls Too Much Focus in a Conflicted Family Film
description: “Way of the Warrior Kid” tries to deliver two lessons for the price of one, but both shortchange the audience. Adapted from the book of the same na
body:
“Way of the Warrior Kid” tries to deliver two lessons for the price of one, but both shortchange the audience. Adapted from the book of the same name by retired Navy SEAL Jocko Willink, the film traces the dual journeys of a wounded veteran (Chris Pratt) and his bullied nephew (Jude Hill) over the course of a summer in San Diego, but it’s alternately too interested and not interested enough in each of their stories to deliver more than a series of familiar coming-of-age platitudes zhuzhed up with military vocabulary. Director McG layers in a handful of clever flourishes over screenwriter Will Staples’ perfunctory storytelling, but the film better showcases Apple Studios’ prodigious output than it does their commitment to quality.
	

	Pratt plays Jake, a decorated Navy SEAL sidelined by injury and haunted by the loss of a comrade after a failed mission to rescue children taken hostage “by militants overseas.” Convalescing at the San Diego home of his sister Sarah (the infinitely more deserving Linda Cardellini), Jake aims to recover well enough to return to active duty and complete his mission. But when Sarah’s son Marc (Hill) begs him for training to stand up to schoolyard bully Kenny (Levi McConaughey), Jake agrees to put the kid on an exercise regimen — with the provision that Marc also learns how to avoid fighting altogether.

	As a kid who can’t walk from his front door to the school bus without tripping on his own shoelaces, Marc thrills at the chance to develop a bit of muscle, along with some much-needed confidence. But as Marc faces his fears for the first time, Jake’s stiff-upper-lipped attitude to his own pain quickly melts in the warming glow of the pair’s camaraderie. As Jake eyes another tour of duty to go back and finish what he started, Marc begins to realize that prevailing over his tormentor doesn’t have to mean the physical fight he’s been preparing for all summer.
	

	Willink has thus far written five books about Marc and his uncle Jake, so there is clearly an appetite for stories that are both family-friendly and military-adjacent. But condensed to an overlong 106 minutes of screen time, this adaptation of the first in the series treads an awkward line between elements that kids can take away from watching, and those directed at their parents (or uncles). 

	Marc is a kid who loves video games and feels particularly empowered playing a Rock Band stand-in called Band Jam; each time he plays, McG cleverly transforms the world around him to reflect his sense of empowerment. Gen X-ers like Jake, with or without intense military training, will likely have little tolerance for the boy’s preferred method of athletic activity — which is to say, through a gaming console — but Jake seldom meets his nephew at his level, instead instructing him on warrior values, never translating the boy’s interest from the virtual world to the real one.

	As Staples’ script efficiently reveals, Marc’s own father has passed away, prompting Jake to respond, “Okay, that happened.” It’s meant not as a dismissal, but to encourage Marc to move on from the kind of identity-defining loss that lurks in just about everyone’s background, including Jake’s. But 40 years ago, Mr. Miyagi in “The Karate Kid” taught audiences to apply the deeper lesson from a superficial act, and everything here is terribly literal, making it less relatable to a broader spectrum of adolescents who might gain some real perspective from this tale.

	It’s hard to know if Pratt is trying to prove, post-“Guardians of the Galaxy,” that he’s more than a buffoon, or if he’s injecting his signature goofy humor into characters, like Jack, who are meant to be more serious and capable. But this character is an uncomfortable and frequently joyless fit for the guy whose golden-retriever energy elevated Andy Dwyer from comic relief to an essential part of the ensemble on “Parks and Recreation.” Good-looking guys can be funny, but the more fit and conventionally handsome Pratt gets, the less interesting his performances become.

	“Belfast” star Hill seems talented, but it’s hard to know if he’s been given line readings here by his director, or if someone has guided him to act “like an adult” in his performance, turning it into a pantomime of awkward adolescence. Cardellini, meanwhile, frantically fights against all the movie clichés of single motherhood — well-meaning and devoted but frazzled — but the movie is so focused on the relationship between Jake and Marc that there’s not much room for her deeply felt work.
	

	Assuming Staples’ script translates Willink’s book faithfully, the author is to be commended for not simply lapsing into teenage wish-fulfillment and letting Marc teach Kenny a well-needed lesson. But what McG does instead is offer a much bigger, more elaborate and less plausible opportunity for Marc to triumph, which takes the film from the realm of reality — albeit one where foreign militants will wait weeks for the soldier trying to stop them to recover from his injuries — to a sequence from “Spy Kids.” The film is most winning when it’s most grounded — as when it puts the audience in Marc’s shoes, using the camera to make him feel disembodied as he gingerly asks his dream girl on a date. 

	Ultimately, Pratt is too big a star to simply act in support of a story where he isn’t the focus — which ends up being to the detriment of what is really a kid’s tale. Because the film must cater to his movie-star presence, the epiphanies experienced by Marc feel designed for adults to appreciate, offering a pointed reminder that there’s a difference between not talking down to a kid and not talking directly to one. “Way of the Warrior Kid” doesn’t bring enjoyment, empowerment or enlightenment, so much as a sense of, “Okay, that happened.” Either way, a sock in the teeth feels as appropriate a response to somebody throwing your bike into San Diego Bay as spending an entire summer building a psychological profile understanding why they threw it in there in the first place.

schema.headline: ‘Way of the Warrior Kid’ Review: Chris Pratt Pulls Too Much Focus in a Conflicted Family Film

title: ‘The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County’ Renewed for Season 2 at Hulu
description: Hulu is continuing the “Secret Lives” universe. “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County” has been renewed for a 20-episode second season a
body:
Hulu is continuing the “Secret Lives” universe. “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County” has been renewed for a 20-episode second season after a quite successful first season.

	The debut season, which dropped on Nov. 12, drove 35 million hours globally in its first 11 days on Hulu and Disney+; the premiere landed 12% ahead of Season 5 of the flagship series. Overall, the franchise has driven over half a billion total hours globally.
	

	The first season, consisting of eight episodes, followed the lives of dynamic young mothers in Orange County. A spinoff of Utah-set headline-making “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives,” this season’s cast included Ashleigh Pease, Aspyn Ovard, Jen Affleck, Bobbi Althoff, Avery Woods, Salomé Andrea, McCall DaPron, Jordan McClanahan and Madison Bontempo. DaPron’s sister, Mayci Neeley, is a cast member on the original “Secret Lives of Mormon Wives” and made a cameo on Season 1 of the spinoff; Affleck is also a cast member on both series.

	While some of the women — DaPron and McClanahan, in particular — are current members of the Mormon church, not everyone in the group is on the same page about religion. 

	“Technically, I am baptized into the Mormon Church. I don’t identify with being Mormon, but I’ve been to the Mormon Church a million times. There’s so much Mormon influence in my life, even just with getting married at 19 and having kids young — the culture has shaped me so much, whether I like that or not,” Ovard told Variety ahead of the Season 1 debut. “I think there’s so much [the cast] can gain from each other. I mean, everyone is so different, and especially the girls who are active Mormons, there’s so much that they can learn from us girls who are very progressive and very liberal… even though I’m not a Mormon wife, I feel like I definitely have a place on the show, and I think it makes sense that I’m there.”
	

	“The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County” is produced by Jeff Jenkins Productions, with 3BMG and Walt Disney Television Alternative. Executive producers are Jeff Jenkins, Russell Jay-Staglik, Amanda Weinstein, Melissa Bidwell, Brandon Beck, Ross Weintraub, Reinout Oerlemans, Georgia Berger, Lisa Filipelli and Danielle Pistotnik.

              Jagged Edge singer Brandon Casey is facing some disturbing allegations ... with a woman accusing the R&B star of sexually assaulting her multiple times when she was just a child.
      
    
              According to a civil lawsuit, obtained by TMZ, Tyliyah S. Lee claims Casey sexually assaulted her on five separate occasions in Philadelphia when she was between 6 and 10 years old.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Lee says she first met Casey at a community event in 2003, where she showed him a song she'd written called "Walked Out of Heaven" ... which she also accuses him of stealing without giving her credit or compensation.
      

              Jagged Edge released its hit "Walked Outta Heaven" that same year ... though Lee's lawsuit does not include a copyright claim.
      
    
              Lee alleges Casey later sought her out and sexually assaulted her repeatedly ... claiming the alleged abuse left her struggling with severe emotional distress, depression, and anxiety.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              And there's some serious money involved ... while her lawsuit seeks more than $50,000 in damages, court documents show her attorney previously demanded $15 million from Casey.
      
    
              Casey is fighting back ... denying every allegation of wrongdoing in court documents filed November 19, when his attorneys moved the case from Pennsylvania state court to federal court.
      
    
              The lawsuit includes one civil claim for battery, and Lee is seeking compensatory and punitive damages.

description:
U.S. Army in Iowa
                          Bringing the Boom Before the Bird!!!
body:
U.S. Army in Iowa
                          Bringing the Boom Before the Bird!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 23, 2026
                            9:01 AM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 23, 2026
                                10:51 AM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
          Update
  
    
              10:49 AM PT -- President Trump said he will defer to a federal appeals court on whether the administration moves ahead with plans to detonate.
      
    
              Before Americans start blowing up their waistlines with Thanksgiving dinner ... the U.S. Army is planning to blow up nearly 5 tons of explosives in Iowa.
      
    
              According to Iowa Public Radio, the Army has rescheduled its massive detonation of deteriorating lead azide -- a highly sensitive explosive compound -- for Wednesday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown ... just one day before Turkey Day.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
              And this is one holiday blowout that's raising some serious concerns.
      

              The blasts were originally scheduled for Friday, then pushed to Monday ... before the Army settled on Thanksgiving Eve, citing better weather conditions and the need for additional safety precautions.
      
    
              But there's a reason officials aren't eager to keep kicking the explosive can down the road ... the Justice Department has warned that freezing temperatures could potentially trigger an uncontrolled explosion.
      
    
              Meanwhile, environmental groups are fighting the operation in court, raising concerns about toxic lead dust expected to be released into the air.
      
    
              A federal appeals court has temporarily put the operation's environmental permit on hold ... though the Justice Department argues the Army can still proceed under an emergency exemption.
      
    
              Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds has already activated the state's Emergency Operations Center, while the Army says it's working to ensure the blasts are carried out safely.
      
    
              No start time has been announced ... but it looks like Iowa could be getting a serious bang before the holiday feast.

              Lee Fryer -- a wheelchair basketball player who won a silver medal at the 2024 Paralympics with Great Britain -- has been charged with rape in the United Kingdom.
      
    
              According to multiple reports ... Fryer is facing 17 charges, including 11 counts of rape for alleged incidents prosecutors say took place between May 2021 and May 2026.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
              The first alleged rape is said to have taken place in 2021 when Fryer was 18 years old.
      

              Fryer's criminal charges also include the alleged oral, vaginal and anal rapes of a woman in Spain between September 2023 and March 2024.
      
    
              He's also facing sexual assault charges from alleged incidents in South Africa ... and charges of voyeurism, intentional strangulation, assault and controlling or coercive behaviour in an intimate relationship.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Fryer played for the Great Britain Paralympic team in 2024, which narrowly lost the gold medal to the USA in a 73-69 nail-biter.
      
    
              His trial is scheduled for March. If convicted on all counts, he could receive a life sentence.
